claims.text: Alloying CoCrFeNi with approximately 0.5–2 wt.% Y is the proposed intervention.
Adding Y to CoCrFeNi promotes in situ formation of a Y-rich oxide tribofilm during sliding.
The Y-rich oxide tribofilm is continuous across the temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C.
The Y-rich oxide tribofilm is lubricious.
The Y-rich oxide tribofilm remains thermally stable up to 800 °C.
Undoped CoCrFeNi exhibits rising friction and wear at elevated temperatures.
Unstable or ineffective oxide-scale formation causes the elevated-temperature friction and wear of undoped CoCrFeNi.
During high-temperature sliding, Y atoms segregate to the worn surface.
Surface-segregated Y oxidizes preferentially to form an adherent Y-rich oxide layer.
The Y-rich oxide layer reduces direct metal-to-metal contact.
Reducing direct metal-to-metal contact decreases friction and wear.
A minor Y addition does not adversely affect the low-temperature mechanical properties of CoCrFeNi.
The proposed Y concentration provides enough segregation during sliding to initiate oxide formation as temperature increases.
Y-doped CoCrFeNi will have a consistently lower coefficient of friction than undoped CoCrFeNi from room temperature to 800 °C.
Y-doped CoCrFeNi will have lower wear than undoped CoCrFeNi from room temperature to 800 °C.
The predicted benefit is scoped to dry sliding under loads of approximately 5–10 N.
Humidity, lubrication, or loads substantially above 5–10 N may alter the predicted performance.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis asserts a continuous Y-rich tribofilm across the entire room-temperature-to-800 °C range, whereas the mechanism describes preferential oxidation during high-temperature sliding and oxide initiation only as temperature increases. No film-forming mechanism is supplied for room-temperature sliding.

At low temperature the mechanism predicts only that Y will not adversely affect mechanical properties, while the outcome predicts lower friction and wear than the baseline throughout the full range. Non-degradation does not explain the asserted low-temperature improvement.
